newsitem.title: FRANCE: Talks break down between French truckers, bosses.
newsitem.headline: Talks break down between French truckers, bosses.

text.p: Talks broke down early on Friday between haulage bosses and French truckers' unions whose were on strike for a fifth day, blocking roads and petrol depots around the country.
But both sides said they hoped to resume negotiations later in the day about as their conflict began showing increased signs of squeezing the economy.
The truckers are demanding wage rises, shorter working hours and retirement at 55 instead of 60.
Union representatives told reporters they broke off the negotiations at two in the morning (0100 GMT) after a session which began nearly 10 hours earlier.
"Our disagreement with them is total. We must maintain pressure for things to advance," said Claude Debons of the CFDT truckers union.
Debons and fellow union representatives told reporters they wanted the government to become involved in the talks, especially concerning early retirement.
About 50,000 trucks were taking part in the protests according to some unions, and the drivers were bent on continuing their action until their demands were met.

Truckers have singled out Bordeaux, whose mayor is Prime Minister Alain Juppe, as the main focus of protests, causing huge traffic jams on all access roads. Airlines at Bordeaux airport said air freight has been badly hit.
Petrol stations there began closing on Friday because they had not been supplied.
Car-maker PSA Peugeot Citroen said it had reduced shifts at several plants because of a shortage of spare parts, and some supermarkets were running low on supplies.

Motorways in and out of 30 towns and cities across the country were blocked by trucks, recalling a 1992 truckers' blockade that paralysed France in a protest against a new points system for driving licences.
But Paris has largely been spared during this year's protests apart from some disruption on Wednesday.
Toulouse, Lyon, Clermont-Ferrand, Caen, Le Mans and the Franco-German border at Strasbourg were also seriously affected.
